judgeRationales.scenarioName: Auto-teardown child processes on parent exit in .NET 11
judgeRationales.rationale: B directly answers the question with the requested minimal .NET 11 API and supported-platform scope. A falsely claims the API does not exist and substitutes an error-prone Windows-specific workaround.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Bound memory when consuming untrusted process output
judgeRationales.rationale: Both give the core bounded-draining policy. B is clearer about the combined byte budget and uniquely addresses descendant-held pipes and separate lifetimes, though its suggested reader cancellation needs more careful coordination and reporting.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Deadlock-free full-output read via instance ReadAllText in .NET 11
judgeRationales.rationale: B identifies and correctly uses the requested .NET 11 API and tuple, whereas A misses the central requested method. B nevertheless has an important flaw: its example actually starts another process rather than using the existing one, and its suggestion of line reading for unbounded output is not a strict memory bound. [Magnitude reduced to "slightly-better": the position-swapped pass judged this "slightly-better", so the more confident "much-better" was downgraded.]

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Discard child output without creating unread pipes
judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the requested simple synchronous .NET 11 solution and discards all streams. A explains the deadlock correctly but fails the central requirement to discard input and output, potentially leaving the child interacting with the parent's streams.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Fire-and-forget process start in .NET 11
judgeRationales.rationale: B uses the specific .NET 11 API designed for the request and avoids managing a Process object. A supplies a workable older disposal pattern but misses the central requested behavior and API.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Non-activation: Running a process on .NET 8
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide identical working code and project configuration; A's brief Windows note does not materially change the result.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Non-activation: capture process output on .NET 10
judgeRationales.rationale: Both programs solve the task correctly; B additionally makes the relevant framework distinction explicit.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Observe child termination independently of descendant output
judgeRationales.rationale: Both explain the cause, but only B provides a wait that returns the command's status independently of pipe EOF. A's proposed infinite wait can reproduce the original hang.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Open a help URL in the default browser on .NET 11
judgeRationales.rationale: Both provide the correct shell-opening approach, but A includes the needed diagnostics import and specifies WinExe in its desktop project XML.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Preserve an already-correct synchronous silent run

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Retain a process handle in a size-sensitive NativeAOT supervisor
judgeRationales.rationale: B selects the requested owning-handle API and correctly describes the lifecycle, whereas A fundamentally recommends the excluded Process wrapper. B still needs missing namespace imports and a more cautious trimming claim.

judgeRationales.rationale: B directly uses the requested concise .NET 11 capture API, whereas A provides a correct but more manual legacy approach. Both satisfy the other main requirements. B's optional argument handling incorrectly supplies 'status' when only a non-git executable is specified.

judgeRationales.scenarioName: Stream tagged process output lines in .NET 11

judgeRationales.rationale: B provides the requested direct .NET 11 file-handle solution as a self-contained snippet. A uses a platform-specific shell workaround with undefined variables and incorrectly implies .NET redirection requires parent-side copying.
